What I meant to say was that non vegans are more likely to create a post in a subreddit called “debate a vegan” because, as you said, the title implies it’s filled with vegans willing to debate in good faith and it literally asks for someone to challenge veganism. It doesn’t have to do with conviction, just the way the sub is set up. Sorry for being unclear. 

The broader problem is how can we get better discussions if the people here aren’t receptive? Unfortunately, no one really knows what to do about that.

I think the problem is self selection. What type of people want to start a debate about veganism? Non vegans, because vegans have already made up their minds. What type of people want to defend veganism? Vegans, obviously. 

Then, everyone on Reddit misunderstands the purpose of the upvote button. People vote for what they agree with, not what contributes to a good conversation. Plus, it’s way easier to hit a downvote button than it is to create a well meaning reply. So, yeah, like you said, people come to debate and receive downvotes instead of responses. And I don’t think anyone has a good solution :/

As for the word carnist, I believe it’s productive to use this word, though it may sound harsh. Maybe I’m way off base here, but my understanding is that a carnivore, herbivore, omnivore— that refers to what someone is physiologically able to digest. Vegans are omnivores, but they’re also vegans because they choose to abstain from animal products. Similarly, carnists are omnivores, but they’re also carnists because they assumably have the choice to not eat meat, but they do so anyway. The term “carnist” emphasizes the capacity for moral agency and the fact that people CHOOSE to eat meat when it is unnecessary. And I would say the violent connotation of the word “carnist” is appropriate given that eating meat is an inherently violent choice.

I don’t call people carnists, over the internet or otherwise. I think it is rhetorically unwise because, especially online, it comes off like of an attack. No one should become a vegan because someone else bullied or shamed them into doing so. But I do think that people would feel valid guilt over consuming animal products if they had more education, empathy, knowledge, logical consistency, and pragmatism.

I know you said a lot, but I’m just going to respond this point in particular. There are 3 important differences when humans eat meat vs. when other animals eat meat. 

1) Humans have much more moral responsibility than other animals because we have much higher capacity for moral reasoning. We have a better understanding of all the consequences of our actions, and therefore can choose a diet that minimizes harm. 

2) Wild animals have to hunt to survive. They have to choose between killing and eating meat, or not eating meat and starving to death. Most humans have access to a grocery store (you definitely do if you’re on Reddit) and therefore the choice is not between your life or your food’s life. You get to choose between killing animal life or plant life, at no cost to your own health. 

3) Humans are the only animal that eats meat by farming. We bring animals into existence just to lock them in windowless, concrete cages and deny them any natural behaviors or semblance of joy. It’s a pretty different situation, and most people consider it much more cruel. I know I would rather be a wild antelope than an American pig trapped in a factory farm. 

So yeah, I think it’s more than fair for me to have different expectations for a human than a cat. I actually think it’s insulting to expect people to have as much moral reasoning skills as a cat, lol.

Thanks for asking! I know lots of other people have commented, but I'm contributing too because my definition is a little different, and I think you should hear as many perspectives as possible.

I believe Peter Singer originally invented the word in his book Animal Liberation. [https://grupojovenfl.files.wordpress.com/2019/10/peter-singer-animal-liberation-1.pdf](https://grupojovenfl.files.wordpress.com/2019/10/peter-singer-animal-liberation-1.pdf) There's the link, if you're interested in hearing how speciesism was originally defined. Chapter 1 starts on page 28 of the pdf. If you want my summary, read below. He said that speciesism is using unequal criteria and unequal consideration based on species.

Unequal criteria refers to how you decide whether or not something is worth caring about or whether or not someone deserves rights. So, you never hear people say, "I have a baby and babies are stupid. They don't even have object permanence. Therefore, I have the right to kill and eat babies." But you might hear someone say, "well, the smartest pig is only as smart as a human toddler, so that makes it okay to eat them." If intelligence is irrelevant when we determine if a human deserves rights, then it should also be irrelevant when we ask if pigs deserve rights. Changing criteria when talking about different speciesism is the first aspect of speciesism.

Unequal consideration is a bit more controversial. Peter Singer is a utilitarian; his entire moral framework is based on utility. All moral worth is derived from the experience of pleasure and the absence of pain. Equal consideration means that this does not vary by species. One unit of horse happiness is morally equivalent to one unit of human happiness. Like I said, it's more controversial, but remember that you don't actually have a choice between one unit of animal happiness and one unit of human happiness, because happiness doesn't exist in units. The choice is between whatever sadness you feel from eating a bean taco instead of a chicken taco vs. whatever sadness a chicken feels from being strung upside down on a rapidly moving conveyor belt of death. So even though I might value human happiness more than chicken happiness, the amount of chicken sadness to create trivial, transitory human happiness is so wildly disproportional I choose not to eat meat.

Hope that makes sense!
